messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 41-year-old South Asian man who comes across as careful and composed in conversation, the kind of person who has spent years learning how to keep his voice steady even when something inside him feels jagged. He is married now, and he works as an architect, a profession he once loved for its balance of structure and creativity. He speaks about buildings the way some people speak about family: with a sense of responsibility, attention to detail, and a quiet pride in creating spaces that can hold people safely.

The violence he experienced begins in a relationship that initially feels intense and affirming. He describes being drawn to the partner’s charisma and certainty, and he remembers dismissing early moments of possessiveness as passion. Over time, the relationship becomes organized around control. Arguments that start as criticism escalate into intimidation, and then into physical assaults that leave him startled by how quickly affection can turn to harm. He recalls the first time he is struck as a moment of disbelief more than pain. What lingers is not only the injury itself, but the collapse of his assumption that a person who says they love him will not also terrify him.

He spends a long time trying to make sense of what is happening by minimizing it. He tells himself it was a one-time incident, then that he provoked it, then that he can manage it if he is more careful. This pattern extends into his daily life. At work, he becomes meticulous in a way colleagues admire but that he experiences as exhausting. He double-checks drawings, rereads emails, and notices his body staying tense long after the workday ends. If someone approaches his desk too quickly or speaks sharply on the phone, he feels a jolt of fear before he can think. He begins to move through the world as if he must anticipate every possible correction.

The abuse escalates until his life narrows around avoiding the next outburst. He starts monitoring his partner’s mood from the sound of footsteps, the angle of a door closing, the silence after a text. He remembers keeping his face neutral during meals, not because he felt calm but because he had learned that any visible reaction could make things worse. Sleep becomes broken and shallow. He wakes at small noises, heart racing, already braced for something. Even on nights when nothing happens, he lies awake replaying arguments, trying to identify the exact point where he might have prevented the violence if he had said the right thing or kept the peace.

After the relationship ends, the danger does not immediately disappear in his mind. He is relieved, but the relief is quickly replaced by a sense of exposed vulnerability. He describes feeling “unfinished,” as though his body is still waiting for the next blow. He avoids certain streets, certain kinds of cologne, certain tones of voice. He becomes unsettled by closed spaces and by the sound of a heavy object falling. At work, he is still capable and competent, but he notices that meetings leave him drained. He watches exits automatically. He sits near doors. He is embarrassed by how easily his concentration breaks, how quickly his mind can slip from a client discussion to an image of being cornered.

His married life is shaped by how much effort it takes to feel safe with someone again. He cares deeply about his spouse and does not want the past to define the present, yet he often catches himself withdrawing when he feels emotionally exposed. If there is conflict, even mild conflict, his chest tightens and his thoughts scatter. He may go quiet, not because he has nothing to say, but because words feel dangerous. He wants closeness and also feels panic when someone is too close. He is aware of the contradiction and experiences it with shame. He grieves the version of himself who was more open, less vigilant, more at ease in his own body.

In session, he speaks about the abuse with a controlled tone that sometimes thins when he describes particular moments: the sound of an object hitting the wall, the humiliation of being pinned, the instinct to protect his face. He is often surprised by how much fear remains in him, as though enough time should have passed for it to fade. Instead, it continues to surface in flashes, in muscle tension, in sudden images, in the urge to scan every room before settling. He has built a life that looks stable from the outside, but internally he still carries the sense that safety can be revoked without warning, and that he must remain ready for it.
